strengths: The paper makes a genuinely interesting attempt to connect possibility theory (supremum-based, non-additive uncertainty) with second-order predictive modelling, which is a relatively unexplored direction compared to the crowded EDL literature.

The derivation is mostly self-contained: the possibilistic posterior (Eq. 6), the supremum-based change of variable (Eq. 7), and the maxitive pseudo-divergence objective (Eq. 8) are clearly presented, and Proposition 1 gives a closed-form approximate maximiser, yielding a simple ~10-line loss (Fig. 1) that is easy to adopt.

The evaluation is broad and reasonably thorough: MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, long-tailed CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-10-C distribution shift, and two fine-grained datasets, with 5 seeds, error bars, ablations on the regulariser (Table 6, Fig. 2), and behaviour analyses (Figs. 3-4) that directly probe the epistemic-uncertainty claim (decreasing uncertainty with more data, ID/OOD separation of alpha_0).

The key approximation (Eq. 11) is not left unexamined: Appendix C provides an empirical leave-one-out / perturbed-label analysis supporting the claim that the leave-one-out infimum is approximately independent of p.

The method requires little extra computation or architectural modification compared to DUQ, PostNet, RS-NN, or Fisher-information-based EDL variants, and achieves competitive or best results on most benchmarks, including against recent 2024-2025 baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'principled derivation' is overstated relative to what the final objective actually contains. The rigorous possibilistic machinery (supremum projection, D_max ordering, Danskin updates) is largely bypassed by the high-capacity approximation in Eq. 11, which collapses the surrogate to exp(-l(p,y)) and reduces the method to a Dirichlet-parameterised evidence loss with a heuristic 'spurious evidence' regulariser (Eqs. 14-17). The epistemic measure K/alpha_0 is the standard EDL total-evidence heuristic, so the practical distance from EDL is small, and the theory-vs-practice gap deserves more honest framing.

The approximation chain is loose at multiple points: the infimum-independence assumption (Eq. 11), the D_max 'vanishing divergence' argument (ordering holds implies divergence is zero but says little about what the learned g_psi actually matches), and the handling of conflicting labels via a 'faithful surrogate' that is never tested. The empirical check in Appendix C (S_x ~ 0.25 vs L ~ 320) supports small perturbations but does not directly validate the full infimum-independence claim.

The ablation in Table 6 reports that applying their regulariser to EDL causes complete failure (0.78 accuracy), which is surprising and under-explained; it raises the question of whether reported gains stem from the possibilistic formulation or from an unfavourable EDL configuration, and the paper does not analyse why the regulariser is not transferable.

Evaluation is limited to AUPR-style metrics; standard calibration metrics (ECE, NLL) and Bayesian baselines such as deep ensembles are only partially included (ensemble appears only on fine-grained datasets), making it hard to judge whether the method genuinely improves probabilistic quality beyond OOD ranking.

Some claims are not fully supported: the assertion that the method 'maintains stable, higher accuracy' and gives 'principled foundation' rests on one dataset-size experiment (Fig. 3) on CIFAR-100; broader validation of the epistemic-uncertainty semantics would strengthen the paper.

Minor presentation issues: the justification for why the regulariser R(x) = ||(1-y) ∘ alpha||^2 follows from the possibilistic view is thin (it is introduced as a practical patch to prevent unbounded alpha_0), and the relationship between the learned possibility function's actual shape and the projected posterior is never directly visualised.

strengths: The application of possibility theory (possibilistic Bayes posterior, supremum-based change of variables, maxitive pseudo-divergence) to second-order predictive uncertainty is a genuinely interesting angle, and the preliminary section is clearly written.
The method is remarkably simple in the end: a ~10-line loss (Fig. 1) that drops in for cross-entropy, with a closed-form maximiser (Prop. 1) and no architectural changes or extra forward passes.

The empirical evaluation is broad: MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, long-tailed CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-10-C distribution shift, and fine-grained benchmarks, with 5 seeds, mean±std reporting, and comparisons against a range of recent EDL variants (I-EDL, R-EDL, DA-EDL, F-EDL, RS-NN).

The analysis experiments are persuasive for the practical claims: epistemic uncertainty monotonically decreases with training-set size (Fig. 3, contrasting with EDL's known pathology), and the normalised α0 distributions separate ID from OOD much better than EDL (Fig. 4).
The authors empirically verify their key approximation (Eq. 11) via a leave-one-out fine-tuning study in Appendix C rather than leaving it as an unsupported assumption.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'principled derivation' is substantially weakened by the paper's own approximations. After the sufficient-capacity argument (Eq. 11), the target posterior collapses to g*_x(p|D) ∝ exp(−ℓ(p,y)) — i.e., the relative likelihood of the label. This surrogate contains no parameter-level epistemic information whatsoever, so the parameter-space possibilistic posterior effectively plays no role in the final objective. The resulting loss is then close in spirit to the heuristic Dirichlet-fitting objectives the paper criticises EDL for, and the claimed resolution of the 'rigour vs. tractability dilemma' is overstated.

There is a significant gap between the derived objective and the implemented one. The derivation yields a min-max problem with the pseudo-divergence Dmax (Eq. 8), which is degenerate: it vanishes whenever g_ψ ⪯ g*, so it does not uniquely determine g_ψ. The implemented loss (Eq. 17) instead evaluates log g_ψ at an α-dependent point p̃* = (α−y)/(α0−1) without any maximisation over p, and minimises log g_ψ (which is non-positive) plus a heuristic evidence regulariser. The formal justification for this substitution is not provided, and it is unclear why minimising log g_ψ at p̃* corresponds to enforcing the ordering constraint derived earlier.

The spurious evidence regulariser R(x) = ||(1−y)⊙α||² is itself a heuristic addition, and the ablation result that applying it to EDL causes complete failure (near-zero accuracy, Table 6) is presented as evidence of uniqueness but more plausibly indicates the objective is fragile and method-specific. λ varies by two orders of magnitude across datasets (Table 7), which sits uneasily with the claim of minimal hyperparameter sensitivity.

Baseline comparability is uneven: many numbers are imported from Yoon & Kim (2025) or Chen et al. (2024) under potentially different architectures and training protocols, and several fine-grained baselines are the authors' own reproductions. Test accuracies on fine-grained datasets (e.g., ~47–56% on CUB-200) are well below commonly reported figures for these architectures, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. Only AUPR is reported; no calibration metrics (e.g., ECE) or AUROC are provided, and deep ensembles appear only in Table 5 rather than the main comparison tables.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only promised ('will be available'), and Appendix B, while detailed, omits some optimisation specifics (learning-rate schedules, data augmentation). There is no limitations section discussing the scope of the high-capacity assumption or failure modes of the approximation (e.g., conflicting labels, where the authors admit Eq. 11 may be violated).

The theoretical positioning leans heavily on adjacent recent work (relative-likelihood credal prediction of Lohr et al., 2025; possibility-theoretic decoupling of Hieu et al., 2025), so the incremental conceptual novelty beyond packaging these ideas into a Dirichlet second-order predictor is modest.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel connection between possibility theory and second-order predictors for deep learning, a direction that is underexplored relative to Bayesian and evidential approaches, and situates it well within the related work (EDL, prior networks, credal/relative-likelihood approaches).

The derivation is coherent and mostly self-contained: possibilistic Bayes posterior (Eq. 2), supremum-based change of variables (Eq. 3, 7), the maxitive pseudo-divergence (Eq. 4), Danskin's theorem for the min-max objective, and a closed-form inner maximizer (Proposition 1). The final loss is simple (Fig. 1), computationally cheap, and easy to adopt as a drop-in replacement for cross-entropy.

Experiments are broad: MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, long-tailed CIFAR-10-LT, corruption-based distribution shift (CIFAR-10-C), and fine-grained datasets, with 5 random seeds and comparisons to many recent EDL variants (I-EDL, R-EDL, DAEDL, F-EDL) and RS-NN.

The analysis experiments are informative: the ablations (Table 6) show the spurious-evidence regularizer is specifically matched to the possibilistic objective (applying it to EDL causes failure), the data-scaling experiment (Fig. 3) directly addresses a known pathology of EDL (increasing epistemic uncertainty with more data), and Fig. 4 gives an interpretable view of the evidence separation between ID and OOD samples.
Appendix C empirically probes the key high-capacity approximation via a leave-one-out perturbation study, which is an honest attempt to validate a theoretical assumption.
weaknesses: The central claim of a 'principled' derivation is weaker than advertised. After the sufficient-capacity approximation in Eq. (11), the projected posterior collapses to g*_x(p|D) ∝ exp(−ℓ(p,y)), i.e., the training target depends only on the label. The resulting method is therefore functionally close to an EDL-style evidence-fitting loss, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate why the possibilistic machinery yields better-grounded epistemic uncertainty than the EDL objectives it criticizes for lacking rigor. The framing (heuristic EDL vs. principled DAPPr) overstates the contrast given how much of the theory is discarded in the approximation chain.

Validation of the key approximation (Eq. 11) is thin: it is checked only on CIFAR-100 with one architecture (Fig. 5), and the experiment shows that perturbing one label barely changes the total loss, which is not exactly the same as showing that the constrained infimum is independent of p across the whole simplex (e.g., for implausible p far from the true label).

Empirical superiority is not uniform: on CIFAR-100 OOD detection DAPPr trails F-EDL on both OOD sets (Table 2), and several OOD gains elsewhere are within ~1-2 points. The abstract's 'competitive or superior' is fair, but 'best' claims in the text should be softened accordingly.

Evaluation relies solely on AUPR for confidence estimation and OOD detection; no calibration metrics (e.g., ECE), AUROC, or FPR95 are reported, and baselines are partly copied from prior papers (potentially different setups) rather than uniformly re-run for the CIFAR experiments. A direct ablation of cross-entropy plus the same regularizer (without the possibilistic objective) would strengthen the attribution of gains to the new formulation.

The theoretical objective and the implemented loss differ in notable ways (uniform prior, D_max ordering semantics where divergence vanishes once g_ψ ⪯ g*, requiring αk > 1, softplus+1 parameterization), and the interaction between the Danskin update and the implemented per-sample loss (Eq. 17) is not fully analyzed, e.g., regarding stability or convergence.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code URL in the abstract is missing, no calibration or additional metric details are given, and a limitations section is absent (the impact statement is boilerplate). Minor typos ('establised', 'token from', 'the inner the maximiser') suggest the manuscript needed another polish pass.

strengths: Novel and largely unexplored angle: grounding second-order predictors in possibility theory, with a coherent pipeline from possibilistic Bayes posterior (Eq. 2), supremum-based projection (Eq. 7), maxitive pseudo-divergence (Eq. 4), Danskin's theorem, to a closed-form surrogate maximiser (Prop. 1, derivation in App. A is correct).

Comprehensive and mostly convincing empirical evaluation: CIFAR-10/100, long-tailed CIFAR-10-LT, fine-grained datasets (CUB, Stanford Dogs), TinyImageNet, ImageNet with a frozen ViT, distribution shift (CIFAR-10-C), and LLM fine-tuning (Mistral-7B on OBQA), with 5 seeds, many strong baselines (EDL variants, PN family, DUQ, PostNet, NatPN, RS-NN, ensembles), and a cost/latency table showing DAPPr matches cross-entropy efficiency.

The paper validates its key approximation (Eq. 11) empirically via a leave-one-out fine-tuning analysis (§D, Fig. 7) rather than only asserting the high-capacity assumption, and includes ablations on the regulariser, on λ, and diagnostics (Fig. 5: epistemic uncertainty decreases with data; Fig. 6: α0 separates ID/OOD).

Practical simplicity: the method is a drop-in replacement for cross-entropy (~10 lines, Fig. 1) with no inference overhead, and detailed implementation/hyperparameter information (App. C) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: A substantial gap between the 'principled' framing and the final objective. After the high-capacity approximation (Eq. 11) and the constant c simplification, the reference g*_x(p) ∝ exp(-ℓ(p,y)) is label-driven, and the realised loss (Eq. 17) is essentially a log-Dirichlet likelihood evaluated at a closed-form point plus a spurious-evidence penalty ||(1-y)⊙α||² that is structurally very close to EDL's regulariser. At test time, the aleatoric (1 - max αk/α0) and epistemic (K/α0) measures are the same forms used in EDL. The claim that DAPPr 'fundamentally differs' from EDL (§B) rests more on the derivation narrative than on the operative loss, which weakens the central theoretical claim.

The foundational motivation is contestable. The claim that probability theory 'presumes sufficient knowledge' and is therefore ill-suited for epistemic uncertainty is a philosophical position, not an established fact; Bayesian treatments of epistemic uncertainty are widely accepted as principled. The 'dilemma' framing is somewhat strawman-like, and the paper does not engage with counterarguments (e.g., imprecise probability/credal sets, which the authors cite only tangentially via Lohr et al. 2025).

Several theoretically motivated steps are hand-waved: the claim that gψ initially over-estimates g*_x at its mode and that training 'progressively drives' the mode toward g*_x is asserted without analysis; the interaction case (conflicting labels at the same x) is mentioned but the faithful surrogate is never used or evaluated; the behaviour of D_max under the subgradient/Danskin argument when the inner maximiser is non-unique is not analysed.

Ablation result that EDL with the DAPPr regulariser collapses to near-zero accuracy (Table 6) is surprising and unexplained; it may indicate training instability of that combination rather than genuine incompatibility, and it is used to support strong 'fundamentally different frameworks' conclusions.

Hyperparameter treatment slightly undercuts the 'minimal tuning, low sensitivity' claim: λ varies by two orders of magnitude across datasets (1e-5 to 5e-3) with dataset-specific warmup/linear schedules (Table 7), and baselines are tuned via sweeps while DAPPr's per-dataset λ is also selected.

Performance claims are occasionally overstated: on some OOD benchmarks DAPPr trails F-EDL or ensembles (e.g., CIFAR-100 TinyImageNet 79.11 vs 80.58; several DTD/ImageNet-O entries), so 'superior' should be 'competitive with occasional gains'; also minor issues such as the empty code URL in the abstract and an unlabeled '1' artifact appearing in several figures.

strengths: The paper is ambitious in scope: experiments span CIFAR-10/100, long-tailed CIFAR-10-LT, fine-grained datasets (CUB, Stanford Dogs), TinyImageNet, ImageNet, distribution shift (CIFAR-10-C), and LLM finetuning (Mistral-7B on OBQA), with mean±std over 5 seeds and reasonably thorough baselines including recent methods (F-EDL, R-EDL, RS-NN, NatPN, IB-EDL).

The method is simple and efficient: the loss is ~10 lines of pseudocode, matches cross-entropy in training time, memory, and inference latency (Table 12), which is a practical advantage over PostNet, DUQ, and ensemble approaches.

The paper includes useful analysis beyond headline numbers: ablations on the regularizer and λ, a data-size study (Figure 5) showing epistemic uncertainty decreases with more data, ID/OOD separation of α0 (Figure 6), reliability diagrams, and an empirical leave-one-out validation of the key approximation (Appendix D).

The framing of possibility theory as an alternative foundation for second-order predictors is interesting, and the related-work coverage of Bayesian, evidential, and possibilistic approaches is solid.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is weaker than advertised. Under the high-capacity approximation (Eq. 11), the 'possibilistic projected posterior' collapses to g*_x(p) ∝ exp(−ℓ(p,y)) — i.e., simply the label likelihood. All the possibility-theoretic machinery (possibilistic Bayes posterior, supremum-based projection, maxitive pseudo-divergence) ultimately reduces to a target that depends only on the observed label, not on any measure of model ignorance about x. This substantially undermines the claim that DAPPr provides a 'principled connection between the objective and epistemic uncertainty' — the same criticism the paper levels at EDL and prior networks.

The key approximation (Eq. 11) is strong and only empirically validated on a single dataset (CIFAR-100, Appendix D) via a fine-tuning protocol whose connection to the actual training-time setting is not fully established. The theoretical argument for it is informal, and the violation case (conflicting labels for identical x) is dismissed rather than analyzed.

The divergence D_max(f‖g) = 0 whenever f ⪯ g means the objective provides no pressure to actually match g*_x — only to stay below it. Combined with the softplus(·)+1 parameterization (which forces αk > 1 and thus forbids the theoretical 'total ignorance' state α0 = 0 that the paper's own Section 3 defines), the actually learned uncertainty scale appears to be determined largely by the ad-hoc regularizer R(x) rather than by the possibilistic derivation. This is an internal inconsistency the paper acknowledges but does not resolve.

The practical distinction from EDL is thinner than claimed. The uncertainty measures (aleatoric = 1 − max αk/α0, epistemic = K/α0) are exactly the post-hoc concentration-based interpretations the paper criticizes EDL for, and the spurious-evidence regularizer (Eq. 16) is functionally very close to EDL's KL-based evidence penalty. Section B argues the difference is 'fundamental,' but given that the target reduces to label likelihood, the practical difference largely amounts to a modified loss form and regularizer — a nuance the framing obscures.

Some empirical results are difficult to interpret: applying DAPPr's regularizer to EDL yields near-zero accuracy (Table 6), which is presented as evidence of framework specificity but more plausibly indicates the regularizer is brittle; the large accuracy gains on fine-grained datasets (e.g., +8.9 points over CE on CUB from a loss replacement alone) are surprising and under-analyzed.

The min-max optimization narrative (Danskin's theorem, inner maximizer p*) is largely mooted by the closed-form substitution in Proposition 1, so the optimization story adds complexity without much substance.

Reproducibility is compromised: the abstract states 'Code is available at' followed by no link. Additionally, there are presentation errors (e.g., Section 4.4 refers to 'pipeline in Figure 3' where Figure 3 is the pipeline but the text describing it appears after Table 1; the contribution list says 'competitive' while the abstract claims 'superior').

strengths: Novel and well-motivated angle: grounding second-order predictors (Dirichlet-style) in possibility theory rather than probability addresses a genuine conceptual gap (additive probability vs. non-exclusion under incomplete knowledge), and the paper positions this clearly against EDL and prior networks.

The derivation is largely self-contained and leads to a practical, closed-form objective (Prop. 1) that can be implemented as a ~10-line drop-in replacement for cross-entropy (Figure 1), which is attractive for practitioners.

Empirically broad evaluation: CIFAR-10/100, long-tailed CIFAR-10-LT, fine-grained datasets, TinyImageNet, ImageNet (with a ViT feature extractor), distribution shift (CIFAR-10-C), and an LLM setting (Mistral-7B on OBQA), with reported variance over 5 seeds.

The authors empirically validate their key approximation (the leave-one-out infimum being constant, Eq. 11) via a fine-tuning experiment in Appendix D rather than only asserting it, and include ablations on the regularizer, λ-sensitivity analysis, reliability diagrams, and a cost/latency comparison showing the method matches cross-entropy in efficiency.

The analysis in Figure 5 (epistemic uncertainty decreasing with more data for DAPPr but not EDL) and Figure 6 (α₀ separation of ID vs. OOD) directly probes whether the uncertainty semantics are correct, not just whether AUPR numbers improve.
weaknesses: The 'principled' framing rests on a long chain of approximations: supremum projection (Eq. 7), Danskin's theorem applied to a possibly non-unique inner maximiser, the leave-one-out constant-infimum assumption (Eq. 11) which itself relies on an overparameterisation argument, and a closed-form maximiser valid only under α_k > 1. By the time the final loss (Eq. 17) is reached, the connection to the possibility-theoretic target is indirect, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate that the machinery—rather than simply the new regulariser—is what drives the empirical gains.

The resulting method is very close to EDL: a single-pass Dirichlet predictor whose concentration parameter is interpreted as epistemic uncertainty. Appendix B argues the frameworks are 'fundamentally different', but the practical distinction reduces to the training target p̃* and the spurious evidence regulariser. A stronger ablation isolating each ingredient against an EDL baseline with equally careful tuning is needed.

Fairness concern in the ablation: Table 6 shows 'EDL w/ R' collapsing to near-zero accuracy (0.78 on CUB, 1.53 on Dogs). This looks like a scaling/mis-tuning artifact of applying the regulariser with DAPPr's λ rather than evidence that the regulariser is 'not interchangeable' with EDL's; the λ that suits log g_ψ(p̃*) may be wildly inappropriate for EDL's likelihood scale.

The maxitive pseudo-divergence objective has an unattractive optimisation property the paper itself notes: once g_ψ ≼ g*_α, D_max vanishes and gradients disappear, so nothing actively drives g_ψ toward the projected posterior. The argument that informative initialisation guarantees a useful over-estimation point is plausible but not verified empirically (e.g., no tracking of the ordering violation during training).

Hyperparameter sensitivity claims are somewhat undercut by Table 7: λ varies over more than two orders of magnitude (1e-5 to 5e-3) and two different schedules (warmup vs. linear) are used across datasets, so 'minimal tuning' is overstated.

No dedicated limitations section; assumptions such as Eq. 11 failing in low-capacity regimes and the conflicting-label caveat are mentioned in passing but their practical consequences are not explored.
Several comparisons rely on numbers copied from prior work (e.g., EDL-based rows from Yoon & Kim, 2025) while others are reproduced in-house, which weakens comparability of the main tables.
